stops.name: The Paris-Fontainebleau road, the crash
stops.campa: On the night of the eighth of July his Citroën leaves the Paris road at speed and strikes a tree by the forest of Fontainebleau. He is found thrown clear, skull cracked, senseless on the grass, with a seat cushion under his head, placed by no hand anyone can name; the mystery is canon. For days he lies between life and death at the Prieuré, mother and wife at the bed, the pupils moving on tiptoe through a house where the teacher's body burns like a lamp low on oil. The wonder is double: that such a driver crashed at all, and that the crash did not kill him.

stops.name: Café de la Paix, the office among the waiters
stops.campa: Risen from the crash, he executes the great turn of his life: he clears the Prieuré of half its pupils, dismisses the easy ones, and becomes a writer. His office is a marble table at the Café de la Paix, his staff the waiters who guard his coffee and armagnac; amid the din of the boulevard, he works best, he says, against interruption, as against a grindstone; he fills notebook after notebook in Armenian and Russian with Beelzebub's Tales to His Grandson, a Flood-sized book in which a devil exiled to our solar system explains, to his grandson, everything.
stops.quote: To destroy, mercilessly, without any compromise whatsoever, in the mentation and feelings of the reader, the beliefs and views, by centuries rooted in him, about everything existing in the world.
stops.quote_source: The declared aim of the First Series, All and Everything (Beelzebub's Tales)

stops.name: The Prieuré, the two deaths: the mother and Madame Ostrowska
stops.campa: Death walks the Prieuré's alleys twice. His mother, brought out of the Caucasus through the wreck of nations, dies in 1925 and is laid in Avon earth. Then cancer takes hold of Julia Ostrowska, and the doctors give her weeks; Gurdjieff, by regimens and by work no physician can enter into the notes, holds her alive and present month after month past every sentence, the canon counting it among his quiet miracles, until on 26 June 1926 he lets her go. He says she dies as very few know how to die. Something of the Prieuré's sun goes under the ground with her.

stops.name: The Prieuré lost
stops.campa: The American crash dries the dollar river; Orage has been recalled and tested and lost to marriage; the mortgages devour the estate. In 1932 the Prieuré passes from his hands, and the seller of a hundred carpets cannot buy back his own decade. He walks out carrying what he came with: manuscripts. The Study House with its painted aphorisms is left to the spiders; the fountain of scent goes dry. In the canon the loss reads as the pattern always reads: the container is broken precisely when the contents have outgrown it. The book is nearly finished, and the book, not the château, was the ark.

stops.name: Paris, 'The Herald of Coming Good': the only book he lets loose, then recalls
stops.campa: In the leanest year he publishes the only book of his lifetime, The Herald of Coming Good: part prospectus, part confession, part deliberate stumbling-block, in sentences built like fortifications. In it he tells of the 1911 oath, of hypnotism, of the Institute's aims and his pupils' debts. Then, having sown it, he reverses the gesture no author in Paris can comprehend: he condemns his own book, recalls the copies from circulation, and instructs the pupils that it is not to be read. The canon takes the point as taught: the coming good must be earned, not bought at a kiosk.

stops.name: Café de la Paix, the Rope
stops.campa: Around his café table gathers the strangest chapter of the teaching: the Rope, a knot of brilliant expatriate women: Kathryn Hulme, Solita Solano, Margaret Anderson, Jane Heap of the Little Review, Elizabeth Gordon, whom he binds together like climbers on one mountain line, telling them that on the inner journey each must haul and be hauled. He teaches them by food, insult, tenderness and exercises given over armagnac at noon; their diaries record a Gurdjieff at full magical strength working in a doll's-house format. Rope by rope, the work learns to live without châteaux.

stops.name: 6 rue des Colonels-Renard, the flat
stops.campa: He settles at last into a small second-floor flat near the Étoile, and the whole cosmology shrinks to fit it perfectly: a dining room where fourteen sit in space for six, a pantry crammed like a bazaar warehouse, a cupboard of spices and dried fish from every latitude of his wanderings. Here the ritual form of the late teaching sets: the reading aloud from Beelzebub, the enormous meals cooked by his own hand, the toasts, the sudden surgical question across the table. Brother Dmitri's death and the schisms pass through; the flat holds. It will hold through worse.

stops.name: The Occupation, the full pantry and the toasts to the idiots
stops.campa: Paris starves under the Occupation, and the flat at the Colonels-Renard does not: the pantry stays unaccountably full, and the canon smiles at how shopkeepers extend infinite credit to the old oriental gentleman on the strength of a Texas oil well that exists chiefly in his telling of it; after the war, American pupils' money makes every merchant whole. Nightly through the war years the table is laid, French pupils gathered by Jeanne de Salzmann eat as nowhere else in the city, and the ritual toasts to the idiots ascend their ladder (ordinary, super, arch), the science of self-seeing disguised, once again, as a feast.
stops.quote: To the health of all ordinary idiots.
stops.quote_source: The first toast of the ritual of the idiots, as kept at his table (recorded by Bennett, Hulme, and the Paris groups)

stops.name: Near Montargis, the second crash survived
stops.campa: On the road in early August a lorry driven by a drunk smashes into his car near Montargis. An ordinary man of seventy-odd dies in such wreckage; Gurdjieff, ribs staved, black with bruises, lungs filling, is carried home, and that same evening comes to table, sits upright by an act witnesses describe as watching a man rebuild himself joint by joint, and commands the household to serve dinner. Within days he reopens the Movements. The second crash becomes the signal for the last great gathering-in: he sends word that all the scattered groups, Ouspensky's orphans included, are to come to him.
stops.quote: Tonight you come dinner. I must make body work.
stops.quote_source: Spoken to J. G. Bennett on the day of the 1948 crash; recorded in Bennett, Witness

stops.name: New York, the Hotel Wellington winter
stops.campa: In December he crosses to New York for the last American winter and holds court in a suite at the Hotel Wellington: the old American pupils return, Orage's people, the Toomer circle, the children of the Prieuré grown, and new ones crowd the corridor. He cooks for dozens on hotel burners, reads Beelzebub aloud, names his heirs' tasks, and settles the great practical matter: the contract for the publication of Beelzebub's Tales, the ark finally to be launched. To pay for it all he sells, with both hands, the futures he no longer needs. Bravo, America: the word of this visit is harvest.

stops.name: Lascaux, the painted cave read
stops.campa: In the last summer he motors south with pupils, Bennett among them, to the newly opened cave of Lascaux. Bent under the low rock, the old man reads the great aurochs and the swimming stags not as the savants read them but as he read the dances of the Sarmoung: as script. He disputes the scholars' twenty thousand years, dates the work by his own chronology to after the loss of the drowned civilization, and tells Bennett the painters were a brotherhood leaving a message for those able to receive it. The seeker's last expedition is to the oldest library he ever entered.

stops.name: Salle Pleyel, the last Movements class
stops.campa: Through October the body visibly founders, the legs swollen tight, the skin gone grey, and still he comes to the Salle Pleyel and drives the Movements classes from his chair, cane striking the floor, building the new series meant for the film that will preserve the dances when he is gone. Pupils see him gather force for each command out of nowhere that medicine knows about. The last class is held days before the end: the library of the Sarmoung, transmitted to the final shelf, in a rented Paris rehearsal hall, by a dying man counting the beat.
